name: Periwinkle
lede: Periwinkle is a light, slightly purplish blue named for the flower, and it sits where blue becomes lilac, which is why the books call it purplish blue, lilac-blue and, for one famous suit, argue over whether it is purple at all.

sections.title: The blue of a flower
sections.body:
Paterson defines periwinkle as a purplish blue and periwinkle blue as a light purplish blue, and he gives *pervenche* blue as the French term for the flower's color [1]. St Clair's glossary agrees on the neighborhood, calling it a lilac-blue after the flower [2]. It lies between [[blue]] and [[lilac]].

St Clair also records that a dusty periwinkle shade called electric blue came into vogue in the late 19th century, around the time Swan and Edison were working on electric light [3].

sections.title: A flower in the poems
sections.body:
The flower is old in European poetry [4][5]. Chaucer's *Romaunt of the Rose* places the violet and the fresh periwinkle among spring flowers [4]. Pastoureau quotes a similar medieval garden in which violets and fresh periwinkles stand beside white, yellow and vermilion flowers [5].

Greek writers are a warning about names. Pastoureau notes that they described the iris, periwinkle and cornflower with words for red, green or black, not blue; Pastoureau notes that Greek color words often conveyed qualities of light or material more than true color [6].

sections.title: Is it purple?
sections.body: Garfield tells of a defense lawyer's double-breasted suit whose color a reporter's research assistant tried to match to a Crayola crayon: the closest was periwinkle, while courthouse onlookers opted for purple [7]. The lawyer insisted the suit was blue, adding that it should not be called mauve [7].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The swatch #A3A8EE falls within a color distance of 6 of only 8 paintings in our archive of 23,781, as photographed [8]. The largest cover is about 45 percent of a 1913 Frieseke flower still life, and the earliest match is a 1637 Claude Lorrain landscape [8]. A periwinkle this clear is uncommon in these photographs of aged, varnished paintings.
